siding_exposure_m.note: INVENTED WITHIN A STOCK SET, NOT DERIVED. No source states the exposed face of any Chicago building's siding. The value is one of four period mill sidings — 4.5, 5, 5.5 or 6 in to the weather; this roof wears 6 in — dealt in this building's own parcel recipe: drawn on this record's stable key from the stocks its household class may hang (5 in, 5.5 in or 6 in; T-1839, docs/LIBERTIES.md L352), then advanced within them so that no roof of the parcel standing within 60 m hangs the same course. It is NOT keyed to a construction season the way the named buildings' stocks are: this record's 1835-01-01 is the programme's count-unit convention and not a date anything was built, so keying to it would deal every anonymous roof in the town one stock. The separation is the surface variety T-0049 reconstructs, not a claim about 1835. docs/LIBERTIES.md L148 owns the invention and the recipe half is recorded beside it, under `tools/siding_stock.py`.

The roof's own existence, position and footprint remain conjectural and are unchanged by the seating — it is still a count-unit of the 665-roof programme, adopted rather than raised, so nothing was drawn off the reconstruction order book. persons.name: William Barry
persons.note: A CONTEMPORARY CHICAGO PAPER OF 1833-1835 PRINTS THIS PERSON BY NAME IN THE TOWN. Read from death_notice, newspaper_1833_1835. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1b), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. newspaper_1833_1835 names this person at Chicago by 17 September 1834 and nothing says when they came. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the person was at Chicago by 1 July 1835 on this record's own evidence. No figure is drawn (L1). THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Barry, Mrs. William Tayl or | Letter. | May 2, 1888. | Dismissed.” (second_presb_0422, printed page 178), admitted 1888-05-02 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Barry' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins W. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE LINE IS A MARRIED WOMAN'S ENTRY, and the crosswalk's own Mrs rule governs what it can have met: “a line flagged a_married_womans_entry that meets a MAN in the 1835 layer has met his name, not him: it corroborates that the name was a Chicago name in the 1840s and it does not put that man on this roll.” The match is filed rather than suppressed, because a suppressed match is invisible and a flagged one can be argued with. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

citations.citation: The Chicago Democrat. Vol. I, No. 1 (November 26, 1833) through Vol. II, No. 18 (August 26, 1835). Chicago, Ill.: John Calhoun, editor and publisher. Seventy-three issues, OCR-assisted research transcriptions from page scans.
what_it_supplies: that a named trade was being carried on in Chicago in a named week, and often where
self-reported addresses, which are the strongest address evidence this project has: the advertiser was paying, and his customers had to find him
dissolution, removal and replacement notices — the only thing that keeps a documented business out of the 1835 town under the owner's ruling 3
post-office letter lists, naming residents by the hundred (ruling 1: a listed name mints a resident candidate, flagged letter_list_only)
the village and later town ordinances, printed complete — the 7 November 1833 code is the richest single item in the run
arrivals and clearances, which date the piers and the harbour as working structures
public notices that fix a building as a polling place, an auction site or a meeting place on a given day
the paper's own imprint, self-reported: the corner of South Water and Clark streets
twenty-one months of continuous weekly attestation ending three weeks before the scene date, including the issue printed on 1835-07-01
what_it_does_not_supply: any building's form, material, storey count, fenestration or dimensions — an advertisement describes a trade, not a building
the specific corner of any junction it names: 'on the corner of' does not say which of the four
anything at all from an engraving — see trap 1; the cuts are the printer's stock
proof that a business named in 1833 or 1834 still stood on 1835-07-01; that is ruling 3's survival liberty, and it is a liberty
an argument from silence, unless corpus.json shows the issues either side of the silence are both in the deposit
a reading that outranks a scan read of the same passage — see ruling 2 and the C. & I. HARMON case
a citation without an issue page and column

citations.citation: "OBITUARY. Names, places, dates, and ages at death of some of Chicago's Old Settlers, prior to 1843, and other well-known citizens who arrived after 1843, together with others prominently connected with Illinois history", in Robert Fergus, Directory of the City of Chicago, Illinois, for 1843, Fergus Historical Series No. 28 (Chicago: Fergus Printing Company, 1896)

transcribes.work: OBITUARY — names, places, dates and ages at death of Chicago's Old Settlers, printed by Robert Fergus in his 1896 reprint of the Directory of the City of Chicago for 1843
transcribes.note: The compiler is fifty-three years and more after most of the deaths he lists, and his own preface calls the 1843 canvass behind the directory 'careless and indifferent'. The list carries this project's only body of ages at death, and through them its only body of derived birth windows.

what_it_supplies: a date of death for 725 named people the compiler connects with Chicago
an age at death for 608 of them, printed as the volume prints it — 'aged 40', 'a. 89½', 'aged 82-2-15'
through that age, an interval the birth falls in: 599 derived birth windows, 166 of them narrow enough to name a single year
a trade or office for 325 of them, and a place of death for 358 who did not die in Chicago
four printed dates of birth, which are documented and not derived
what_it_does_not_supply: arrival before 1843 — the list's own header says it also names 'other well-known citizens who arrived after 1843, together with others prominently connected with Illinois history', and Gov. Richard Yates, Henry Ward Beecher, Marquette and La Salle are all printed in it
residence in Chicago on 1 July 1835, which nothing in the list speaks to
a year of arrival, which the list never prints

citations.citation: Chicago · July 1835: Building Inventory and Architectural Reconstruction Specification. Prepared for Kevin Haas, August 2026.
what_it_supplies: A 665-roof production target with independently reconcilable group, district, level, and construction totals.
Thirty-five architectural family definitions with dimensional and massing bands.
District character, spacing, variation, finish, and chronology constraints for a July 1835 reconstruction.
A required distinction between named documentary landmarks and anonymous inferred infill.
what_it_does_not_supply: A surviving July 1835 building census or parcel-by-parcel roof register.
Exact locations, dimensions, appearance, occupants, or construction dates for anonymous roofs.
Authority to replace stronger building-specific evidence already represented in the dataset.

citations.citation: The Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, June 1st, 1842, to June 1st, 1892 (Chicago: Knight, Leonard & Co., 1892), John C. Grant, editor — the semi-centennial volume of the congregation, read from the Princeton Theological Seminary copy digitised by the Internet Archive as item secondpresbyterian00chic
what_it_supplies: 2,255 lines of a Chicago church roll running from 1 June 1842 to 1892 — a name, how the member was admitted (profession or letter), the date, and for the closed roll a remark (dismissed, deceased, ordained).
962 distinct surnames, of which 938 lines carry a surname this project already holds from the town of 1835.
The founding cohort of 1 June 1842, which is where the overlap with the 1835 town is thickest: W. H. Brown, George W. Dole and Mrs A. N. Fullerton are all on the first day's roll.
A dated Chicago appearance for a surname, which is exactly the kind of second source the resident sweep files as a lead.
what_it_does_not_supply: An 1835 residency, or any part of one. The earliest line on the roll is seven years after the scene date and the ratified ladder never makes an 1835 resident from a later appearance alone.

A woman's own name, much of the time. The roll sets a wife as `Mrs.` followed by her HUSBAND'S name — `Fullerton, Mrs. A. N.` — so a line that meets a man in the 1835 layer has met his name and not him, and the crosswalk flags every such line.
A death or a departure that can be dated. `Deceased` and `Dismissed` are the state of the roll at its closing on 1 June 1892, not events with dates of their own.
An address, a trade or a household. The roll carries none of the three.
